name: Hangzhou
info: Hangzhou is a city in northwestern Zhejiang province, China, at the southern end of the Grand Canal. Established as a county seat under the Qin, it was the capital of the Southern Song and is now the provincial capital.

facts.founded: Established as the county of Qiantang by the First Emperor of the Qin, in 221 or 222 BCE; made the seat of the prefecture of Hang under the Sui in 589 CE, from which the name Hangzhou came.
facts.where: At the southern end of the Grand Canal and the head of Hangzhou Bay, north of the Qiantang River and beside West Lake, in northwestern Zhejiang province, China.
facts.known: The Southern Song capital Lin'an; West Lake and the causeways of Bai Juyi and Su Shi; the southern end of the Grand Canal; a population said to have made it the largest city in the world; accounts by Marco Polo, Odoric of Pordenone and Ibn Battuta; Longjing tea; the fires of the Song city
facts.today: Hangzhou is the capital and most populous city of Zhejiang province and a sub-provincial city in the Yangtze River Delta.

t: Hangzhou began as the Qin county of Qiantang, became a prefectural seat under the Sui in 589 and was joined to the north by the Grand Canal, which reached its full length by 609.
From 1132 until the Mongol conquest of 1276 it was the capital of the Southern Song as Lin'an, and its population grew far beyond its walls, with estimates of more than one million.

Under the Yuan and later dynasties it remained a commercial and administrative centre, its harbour silted up by the middle of the Ming, and the Taiping, warlords and Japanese occupation each brought damage or contest in the 19th and 20th centuries.
dyk: Hangzhou's reputation among Europeans was such that it was the intended destination of Christopher Columbus's first voyage to the Americas in 1492 and 1493.

sections.origins:
Hangzhou stands at the southern end of the Grand Canal and at the head of Hangzhou Bay, in northwestern Zhejiang province, with its centre built around the eastern and northern sides of West Lake, just north of the Qiantang River. People lived in the region long before any city. The Neolithic Hemudu culture inhabited Yuyao, 100 km south-east of Hangzhou, as far back as seven thousand years ago, and rice was first cultivated in southeast China during that time. Excavations have established that the jade-carving Liangzhu culture, named for its type site just northwest of the present city, inhabited the area immediately around it about five thousand years ago.

The first of Hangzhou's present neighbourhoods to appear in written records was Yuhang, which probably preserves an old Baiyue name. The First Emperor of the Qin established Qiantang as a county under the direction of Kuaiji Commandery, now Shaoxing, in the area of the Wulin Mountains and the Wulin Lakes. Under the Han the same area was known as Wulin. In 589 CE the Sui made it the seat of the prefecture of Hang, which entitled it to a city wall, built two years later. By a longstanding convention also seen in Guangzhou and Fuzhou, the city took the name of the area it administered and became known as Hangzhou.
sections.growth:
Hangzhou lay at the southern end of the Grand Canal, which extends to Beijing and evolved over centuries, reaching its full length by 609. In 610 the Jiangnan Canal was dredged and widened along an existing channel to connect Suzhou with Hangzhou. In the Tang dynasty the poet Bai Juyi, as governor, saw that the farmland nearby depended on the water of West Lake and that its old dyke had collapsed through negligence, leaving the farmers in severe drought. He ordered a stronger and taller dyke with a dam to control the flow, and the livelihood of local people improved over the following years.

In the tenth century Hangzhou, then named Xifu, was one of the three great bastions of culture in southern China, with Nanjing and Chengdu. The leaders of Wuyue were noted patrons of the arts, particularly of Buddhist temple architecture and artwork, and the city drew scholars from throughout China and conducted diplomacy with neighbouring Chinese states, Japan, Goryeo and the Khitan Liao dynasty. In 1089 the poet and governor Su Shi used 200,000 workers to build a causeway 2.8 km long across West Lake, made of mud dredged from the lake bottom.

Under the Southern Song, commercial expansion, an influx of refugees from the north and the growth of the official and military establishments increased the population, and the city developed well outside its 9th-century ramparts. The city remained an important port until the middle of the Ming era, when its harbour slowly silted up.
sections.rulers:
Qiantang was a county of the Qin, and the area was called Wulin under the Han. The Sui made it a prefectural seat in 589. In the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period Hangzhou, then called Xifu, was the capital of the kingdom of Wuyue. The Southern Song chose it as their capital in 1132, after most of northern China had been conquered by the Jurchens in the Jin-Song wars and the imperial family had retreated south from Kaifeng, captured in the Jingkang Incident of 1127. Emperor Gaozong moved to Nanjing, then to modern Shangqiu, then to Yangzhou in 1128, and finally to Hangzhou in 1129.

From 1132 until the Mongol invasion of 1276 Hangzhou remained the capital of the Southern Song and was known as Lin'an. It was the seat of the imperial government, a centre of trade and entertainment and the nexus of the main branches of the civil service. The Mongols took it in 1276. The capital of the new Yuan dynasty was Dadu, now Beijing, but Hangzhou remained an important commercial and administrative centre for the Yuan's southern territory. Under the Qing it was the site of an imperial army garrison.

After the collapse of the Qing, warlords, particularly those of the Anhui and Zhili cliques, contested the city until the Kuomintang's Northern Expedition. The Republic of China then administered it more fully from 1927 to 1937. Japan occupied it from 1937 to 1945, the Kuomintang returned and governed until 3 May 1949, and then the People's Liberation Army entered and the city came under Chinese Communist Party control.
sections.life:
When the Southern Song made Hangzhou a permanent capital, its imperial palace, modest in size, was expanded in 1133 with new roofed alleyways and in 1148 with an extension of the walls. The city walls, of tamped earth and stone, were 30 feet high and 10 feet thick at the base, with 13 gates and several towers, and covered four miles north to south and only one mile east to west. Philosophers, politicians and men of letters, among them the poets Su Shi, Lu You and Xin Qiji, came to live and die there, and the scientist Shen Kuo was born there and buried in the Yuhang district. Arab merchants lived in the city during the Song, when ocean trade took precedence over land trade, and a Persian settler built the Phoenix Mosque.

Travellers of the Yuan period described the city as one of the foremost in the world. Marco Polo, who supposedly visited in the late 13th century, called it greater than any in the world, although his account greatly exaggerates its size. Odoric of Pordenone also called it the greatest city in the world, and noted that bread, pork, rice and wine were abundant. Ibn Battuta visited in 1345 and noted the many well-made, painted wooden ships on the canals,.

In 1848 Hangzhou was described as the stronghold of Islam in Zhejiang, with several mosques bearing Arabic inscriptions. It was an important centre of Chinese Jewry as late as the 16th and 17th centuries, and its Immaculate Conception Cathedral dates back 400 years to the Ming. Lingyin Temple was founded in 326 CE. Residents speak the Hangzhou dialect, a Wu dialect.
sections.crises:
Hangzhou was particularly vulnerable to fire, because of its large population and densely crowded, often multi-storey wooden buildings. Major fires destroyed large sections of the city in 1208, 1229, 1237 and 1275. The fire of 1237 alone destroyed 30,000 dwellings. The worst was that of 1208, which burned for four days over a diameter of three miles and burned 58,097 houses, killing 59 people. To combat the threat, the city built storage buildings that were rented out to merchants and patrolled by watchmen at night, and it was enclosed by water on all sides. The government also set up an elaborate fire-fighting system, with watchtowers, lantern and flag signals to identify the source of the flames and direct the response, and more than 3,000 soldiers charged with putting out fires.

In 1276 the advancing Mongol armies of Kublai Khan besieged and captured Hangzhou, three years before the final collapse of the Southern Song. Historian Patricia Buckley Ebrey noted that the Mongols killed the Jurchen Wanyan royal family by the hundreds in the siege of Kaifeng in 1232 but spared Hangzhou, including the Zhao royal family of the Southern Song. The Mongols rehired Southern Song officials.

In 1856 and 1860 the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom occupied Hangzhou, and the city was heavily damaged during its conquest, occupation and eventual reconquest by the Qing army. Japan occupied it from 1937 to 1945. During the late Cultural Revolution Hangzhou was the stage of labour unrest and factional fighting known as the 1975 Hangzhou incident.
sections.legacy:
Hangzhou is counted among the ancient capitals of China, and its poets and governors left marks on its landscape. Bai Juyi had willows and other trees planted along his dyke at West Lake, which became a landmark. The West Lake Cultural Landscape, the Grand Canal, designated in 2014, and the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City are three UNESCO World Heritage Sites in the city. Around the lake stand pagodas and temples, among them Lingyin Temple, the Baochu Pagoda, the Leifeng Pagoda and the Yue Fei Temple, built in 1221 to commemorate the general Yue Fei, who died through political persecution.

An old Chinese proverb says that there is Heaven above, and Suzhou and Hangzhou below. Marco Polo described Hangzhou as the city of heaven. The accounts of Marco Polo, Odoric of Pordenone and Ibn Battuta carried the city's name to western readers under forms such as Khinzai, Campsay and al-Khansa. The China Academy of Art and Zhejiang University are among the institutions in the city.

Today Hangzhou is the capital and most populous city of Zhejiang province, a sub-provincial city in the Yangtze River Delta with more than twelve million permanent residents. It hosted the eleventh G20 summit in 2016. The city still keeps its historical and cultural heritage and its natural setting beside West Lake, despite recent urban development.

summary: Hangzhou, at the southern end of the Grand Canal in Zhejiang, began as the Qin county of Qiantang. From 1132 to 1276 it was the Southern Song capital Lin'an, and travellers described it as one of the foremost cities in the world. It is now the capital of Zhejiang province.
references: Arthur Cotterell, The Imperial Capitals of China: An Inside View of the Celestial Empire (Pimlico, 2007)
Jacques Gernet, Daily Life in China on the Eve of the Mongol Invasion, 1250–1276 (Stanford University Press, 1962)
notes: Only the city's own article was available (no hangzhou-history file).
FOUNDING YEAR: the lead says 221 BC, the Early history section 222 BC. I used start -221 with circa true and wrote '221 or 222 BCE' in facts; the origins text gives no year.
WUYUE DATES: the lead gives 923-997, the Tang section 907 to 978. I left the years out of the text and wrote only 'Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period'.
SOUTHERN SONG CAPITAL DATE: the lead says 1138; the Song section says chosen in 1132 (and Gaozong reached Hangzhou in 1129). I used 1132, as the History section and 'from 1132 until 1276' agree.
ANCIENT CAPITALS: the lead says Eight Ancient Capitals, the Tang section Seven. I wrote 'among the ancient capitals' with no number.

Event 1860: the article says 1856 and 1860 it occupied the city; I wrote 'for the second time' (inference from two dates); editor may soften. Event 1208 'worst of the great fires' is from the article. The 609 canal event was dropped to keep eight events.

POPULATION: Britannica 'over 2 million', Gernet 'well over one million by 1276', census of 1270 gave 186,330 families, probably undercounted. I kept only 'estimates of more than one million' in takeaways and left out the 'largest city in the world 1180-1315 and 1348-1358' belief and the Britannica figure in the text; editor may add. The 1348-1358 claim sits oddly beside Yuan period and was left out.
'Hangzhou's 9th-century ramparts' appears in the article; the Sui wall of 591 is also given. Left as the article states it.
The article says Marco Polo 'supposedly' visited; kept as 'supposedly'. The article's guesses about his 'hundred miles' and '12,000 bridges' were left out.
Lingyin Temple founded 326 CE per article (Eastern Jin 'first year of Xianhe'); the article also says 'about 1,700 years'. Kept 326.

The article's claim that Hangzhou 'may have been the original home of the Kaifeng Jewish community' left out as speculative. Also left out: Jewish synagogue lost, Catholic pillars, economy, rankings, tourism, transport, 2022 Asian Games, Covid curfew, 21st-century persecution of Christians, climate, cuisine detail.
The article's remark that the Mongols 'had Han Chinese artisans in Shangdu marry the palace women' left out.
Columbus dyk is the article's statement, unsourced there; editor may prefer to drop it.
